🔷 November 25 - Saint Katherine the Great Martyr of Alexandria 𖥞 🔷

Today we commemorate the Glorious Martyr Katherine of Alexandria. 

Great Martyr Katherine of Alexandria is venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church as a brilliant scholar, ascetic, and steadfast witness to Christ during the early fourth-century persecutions. 

Born into a noble family in Alexandria, Egypt, she mastered Hellenistic philosophy, rhetoric, and science, yet rejected worldly suitors in search of deeper truth. 

Her life changed after she met a wise spiritual Elder and received a vision of the Theotokos holding the Christ Child.

At first, the Christ Child turned away from Katherine because she had not yet received Christian baptism. 

Guided by the Elder, she learned the Christian faith, was baptized, and lived an ascetic life of prayer and devotion. 

In a second vision, Christ welcomed her, called her wise and pure, and placed a betrothal ring upon her finger as a sign of her mystical union with Him.

When the emperor—identified in Orthodox accounts as Maxentius or Maximian—arrived in Alexandria for a grand pagan festival and public sacrifices, Katherine went before him to confess Christ and denounce idolatry. 

Struck by her intellect and poise, the ruler summoned fifty of the empire’s most learned philosophers and rhetoricians to debate her. 

Instead of defeating her, Katherine refuted their arguments with spiritual wisdom, and all fifty came to believe in Christ.

Enraged by the conversion of the scholars, the emperor ordered them executed and placed Katherine under harsh imprisonment and torture. 

Even in captivity, her witness continued to bear fruit. She helped bring the emperor’s wife, Augusta, along with the commander Porphyrios and two hundred soldiers, to faith in Christ, leading to their own martyrdoms.

To break her resolve, the ruler sentenced Katherine to death on a spiked wheel (image 11).

🔷 November 25 - Saint Mercurios the Great Martyr of Caesarea in Cappadocia 🔷 

Today we also commemorate Saint Mercurios the Great Martyr of Caesarea in Cappadocia.

Saint Mercurius was a third-century Roman soldier of Scythian descent who served under Emperor Decius. 

Before a major battle against barbarian invaders, an angel appeared to him and placed a sword in his hand, promising victory. 

Mercurius led the troops to triumph and defeated the enemy king, earning high military rank and imperial favor.

When Emperor Decius called for pagan sacrifices to celebrate the victory, Mercurius refused and openly declared himself a Christian. 

He laid down his military belt and cloak, rejecting his worldly honors for Christ. 

He endured severe tortures—including fire and scourging—while an angel and the Lord strengthened and healed him in prison.

Enraged by this insubordination, Decius ordered the young general to be subjected to brutal tortures. 

Mercurius was stretched between four pillars, slashed with knives, and burned over an open fire, yet he remained steadfast in his faith. 

When his captors threw his broken body back into prison, an angel appeared and miraculously healed his wounds, leaving him completely restored the next day. 

Fearing that Mercurius’s popularity among the Roman soldiers and citizens might spark a revolt, Decius had him bound in chains and sent back to his homeland of Caesarea in Cappadocia to be executed.

Around the year 250 AD, at roughly twenty-five years of age, Mercurius was beheaded in Caesarea after receiving a final comforting vision from Christ.

🔷 November 26 - Saint Stylianos the Monk of Paphlagonia 👶🔷

Today we commemorate Saint Stylianos the Monk of Paphlagonia , the patron Saint of Children. 

Saint Stylianos of Paphlagonia was a Christian ascetic and hermit who lived in Asia Minor (modern-day Turkey) between the fourth and seventh centuries. 

Born in the city of Adrianopolis, he inherited a considerable fortune upon the death of his parents, though some traditions describe his upbringing as humble in material wealth yet rich in faith. 

Driven by a deep love for Christ and compassion for the suffering, Stylianos distributed all of his worldly possessions to the poor and entered a monastery to dedicate his life entirely to God.

Inside the monastery, Stylianos practiced intense asceticism, fasting, and prayer. 

His extraordinary spiritual zeal and humility soon surpassed those of his fellow monks, unintentionally provoking their jealousy and hostility. 

Seeking peace and uninterrupted communion with God, Stylianos left the monastic community and retreated into the wilderness, where he took up residence in a solitary cave.

Despite his desire for solitude, Stylianos did not completely abandon the surrounding communities. 

Known far and wide for his warm, perpetually smiling countenance, he regularly left his cave to visit nearby villages, offering spiritual counsel and comfort to the troubled. 

Following a profound spiritual experience in prayer, he discovered a divine gift for healing, beginning when he laid hands on a gravely ill child and restored the child to health. Word of his holiness spread rapidly, drawing sick and suffering pilgrims from across the region to his wilderness retreat.

Stylianos became especially renowned for his devotion to children, earning a reputation as their guardian and protector. Parents frequently entrusted their young ones to his care for spiritual guidance and physical healing, prompting him to enlist fellow hermits and establish an early form of a day-care center

🔷 November 26 - Saint Nikon Metanoeite 🔷

Today we also commemorate Saint Nikon Metanoeite. 

Saint Nikon the Metanoeite was a tenth-century Byzantine monk, itinerant missionary, and saint venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church. 

Born into a wealthy family in Pontus or Argos, he renounced his worldly inheritance as a young man and entered the Khrysopetro monastery. 

There, he dedicated twelve years to extreme asceticism, prayer, and penance until his abbot sent him out into the world to preach.

Nikon earned the Greek epithet Metanoeite—meaning “Repent!”—because he opened every sermon with that urgent command. 

Rather than relying on brief emotional displays of remorse, he taught that genuine repentance required ongoing prayer, self-denial, almsgiving, and confession. 

His persistent message, combined with his gentle demeanor and reputed miracles, gradually won over skeptical crowds wherever he traveled.

Following the Byzantine reconquest of Crete from Arab rule in 961, Nikon launched a major mission on the island to re-evangelize a population that had lived under Islamic governance for over a century. 

Finding that local Christian traditions had eroded and churches had fallen into ruin, he adapted his preaching style, using wit and patient instruction to guide former converts back to Christianity.

After departing Crete, Nikon journeyed through mainland Greece—visiting Athens, Euboea, Thebes, and Corinth—before settling in Sparta in the Peloponnese. 

In Laconia, he rebuilt churches, founded a prominent monastery dedicated to Christ the Savior, and played a decisive role in introducing Christianity to the isolated Mani Peninsula. 

Tradition also credits his prayers with delivering Sparta from a devastating plague, though his hagiography notably records that he demanded the expulsion of the city’s Jewish population as a precondition for his intercession.

Nikon remained in Sparta until his Repose in the Year 998 AD , leaving behind a lasting monastic legacy

🔷 Happy Thanksgiving 🍁🔷

Today Brothers and Sisters In the Orthodox Church, thanksgiving is not just a single day on the calendar—it is the very heart of our worship. 

The word Eucharist comes from the Greek word for thanksgiving, reminding us that every time we gather for the Divine Liturgy, we offer back to God what He has given us: our lives, our bread, our wine, and our praise. 

True thanksgiving lifts us above selfish appetites and unites us with God and one another.

When our hearts are full of gratitude to God, it naturally changes how we love our neighbors. 

Ingratitude turns us inward and makes us cling to what we have, while thankfulness opens our hands and hearts. Saint John Chrysostom teaches that what we do not need belongs to those who are in need. 

Loving more means turning our gratitude into concrete acts of mercy, sharing our time, and caring for the poor and lonely around us.

True Christian thanksgiving also calls us into deeper fellowship with one another. We are not meant to walk the path of faith alone; we are members of one Body in Christ. 

Fellowship grows when we forgive quickly, listen patiently, and welcome others without judgment. 

Even during seasonal fasts, such as the Nativity Fast, sharing meals wisely, praying together, and checking in on fellow parishioners strengthens the bond of our community.

Building this kind of love and fellowship takes daily practice rather than waiting for a special occasion. 

Simple habits—like thanking God morning and evening, praying for those who frustrate us, or calling someone who has been absent from church—keep our hearts soft and attentive.

Let us carry a spirit of thanksgiving out of the church doors and into our homes, workplaces, and neighborhoods. 

When we thank God for every gift—including the people placed in our lives—we love more generously and build true fellowship. 

May our gratitude always bear fruit in active love, shared meals, and genuine care for one another.
.

🔷 November 26 - Saint George of Chios, the New Martyr 🔷

Today we also commemorate Saint George of Chios, the New Martyr. 

Saint George of Chios, the New Martyr , was born on the Greek island of Chios in the late 18th century to pious Orthodox Christian parents, Paraskevas and Aggerou. 

Orphaned of his mother at a very young age, he was apprenticed to a woodcarver in his childhood. 

While traveling away from home with other youths, the young boy was caught stealing fruit from a garden in Kavala and brought before an Ottoman judge. 

Terrified of severe punishment, he yielded to pressure, converted to Islam, and was given the name Ahmed.

Shortly after this forced apostasy, the ten-year-old boy was overcome with remorse and returned to Chios in tears, confessing his regret to his father. 

Because leaving Islam was punishable by death under Ottoman law, his father secretly took him across the sea to Kydonies (modern-day Ayvalık) in Asia Minor. 

There, George was placed under the care of a devout Christian farmer, where he lived quietly for over a decade, repenting of his childhood denial and strengthening his Christian faith.

By the age of twenty-two, George had grown into a pious young man and became engaged to a local Christian woman. 

However, a financial quarrel broke out between George and his fiancée’s brother. 

Seeking revenge, the brother betrayed George to the Ottoman authorities, exposing him as an apostate from Islam who had returned to practicing Christianity.

Arrested and thrown into prison, George was subjected to seventeen days of brutal torture as officials tried to force him to renounce Christ once more. 

Far from breaking his spirit, the suffering deepened his resolve, and he declared that he had been born a Christian and would die as one. 

On the night before his execution, a priest secretly administered Holy Communion to him in his cell while local Christians kept an all-night vigil praying for his endurance.

🔷 November 26 - Saint George of Chios, the New Martyr 🔷

Today we also commemorate Saint George of Chios, the New Martyr. 

Saint George of Chios, the New Martyr , was born on the Greek island of Chios in the late 18th century to pious Orthodox Christian parents, Paraskevas and Aggerou. 

Orphaned of his mother at a very young age, he was apprenticed to a woodcarver in his childhood. 

While traveling away from home with other youths, the young boy was caught stealing fruit from a garden in Kavala and brought before an Ottoman judge. 

Terrified of severe punishment, he yielded to pressure, converted to Islam, and was given the name Ahmed.

Shortly after this forced apostasy, the ten-year-old boy was overcome with remorse and returned to Chios in tears, confessing his regret to his father. 

Because leaving Islam was punishable by death under Ottoman law, his father secretly took him across the sea to Kydonies (modern-day Ayvalık) in Asia Minor. 

There, George was placed under the care of a devout Christian farmer, where he lived quietly for over a decade, repenting of his childhood denial and strengthening his Christian faith.

By the age of twenty-two, George had grown into a pious young man and became engaged to a local Christian woman. 

However, a financial quarrel broke out between George and his fiancée’s brother. 

Seeking revenge, the brother betrayed George to the Ottoman authorities, exposing him as an apostate from Islam who had returned to practicing Christianity.

Arrested and thrown into prison, George was subjected to seventeen days of brutal torture as officials tried to force him to renounce Christ once more. 

Far from breaking his spirit, the suffering deepened his resolve, and he declared that he had been born a Christian and would die as one. 

On the night before his execution, a priest secretly administered Holy Communion to him in his cell while local Christians kept an all-night vigil praying for his endurance.
